q: A 55-year-old male presents with left-sided chest pain that is reproduced exactly by palpation of the 3rd left costochondral junction. He has no dyspnoea, no radiation, no exertional component, and normal ECG and troponin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Unstable angina — urgent cardiology referral
Costochondritis — NSAIDs, heat, and reassurance
Pulmonary embolism — CTPA
Aortic dissection — CT angiogram
explanation: Costochondritis: localised anterior chest pain reproduced exactly by palpation of the costochondral junction — this is the defining clinical feature. Normal ECG and troponin exclude ACS. No exertional, radiation, or vascular features. Management: NSAIDs (ibuprofen 400mg TDS) for 2–4 weeks, heat, activity modification. Reassurance is critical — many patients fear cardiac disease and the reassurance that the pain is musculoskeletal can be profoundly relieving. Most cases resolve within weeks to months. Local corticosteroid injection for refractory cases. Distinguish from Tietze syndrome (same presentation but with visible swelling at the junction).

q: What distinguishes Tietze syndrome from costochondritis?
options: Tietze affects the lower ribs; costochondritis affects the upper ribs
Tietze syndrome has visible and palpable swelling at the affected costochondral junction; costochondritis has no swelling — tenderness only
Tietze is always bilateral; costochondritis is always unilateral
Tietze requires surgery; costochondritis resolves without treatment
explanation: Both conditions present with anterior chest wall pain at the costochondral junctions. The key distinguishing feature: Tietze syndrome has visible, palpable swelling at the affected junction — usually a single joint, most commonly 2nd or 3rd. Costochondritis has no swelling — tenderness only. Tietze is less common. Both are managed similarly — NSAIDs, heat, local corticosteroid injection for refractory cases, reassurance. Both are benign and self-limiting. Cardiac causes must be excluded in both presentations before a musculoskeletal diagnosis is accepted.

q: A 72-year-old female with osteoporosis presents after a fall. She has point tenderness over the left 6th rib laterally and severe pain with deep inspiration. CXR shows no pneumothorax. SpO2 is 94% on air. She has COPD. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Prescribe NSAIDs and discharge home with GP follow-up in 1 week
Hospital admission — criteria met for admission (elderly, COPD, SpO2 94%, rib fracture); adequate analgesia, incentive spirometry, physiotherapy, oxygen, monitoring for complications
Chest binding for comfort and discharge
CT chest immediately to exclude aortic dissection
explanation: Rib fracture admission criteria: elderly patients, underlying COPD or respiratory disease, SpO2 declining or below baseline, pain uncontrolled with oral analgesia, haemothorax or pneumothorax. This patient meets multiple criteria. Chest binding is contraindicated — reduces tidal volume and worsens atelectasis and pneumonia risk. Hospital management: NSAIDs + paracetamol ± opioids for analgesia; incentive spirometry; chest physiotherapy; oxygen titrated to maintain SpO2 88–92% in COPD; serial CXR to monitor for pneumothorax or haemothorax development; consider intercostal nerve block or thoracic epidural for superior analgesia.

q: A 65-year-old male presents with severe burning left-sided chest pain for 3 days, without a rash. He describes it as an electric, constant burning along a band around the left side of his chest. He has no cardiac risk factors. ECG is normal. Troponin is negative. What diagnosis must be considered and what should be examined for?
options: Musculoskeletal strain — NSAIDs
Herpes zoster (prodromal phase — pain before rash) — examine carefully for early vesicles along the dermatomal distribution; start valaciclovir if suspicion is high even without visible rash
Pulmonary embolism — CTPA immediately
Costochondritis — palpation confirms
explanation: Herpes zoster (shingles) prodromal phase: VZV reactivation causes dermatomal pain 1–5 days before the vesicular rash appears. The pain is typically described as burning, electric, or stabbing in a unilateral dermatomal band distribution. It can be mistaken for cardiac, pleural, or musculoskeletal pain. Key: examine carefully along the dermatomal distribution for early vesicles. If clinical suspicion is high, consider starting valaciclovir empirically (1g TDS for 7 days) even without visible rash — antivirals are most effective when started early. Pre-rash zoster is one of the most commonly misdiagnosed causes of unexplained chest pain.

q: An 80-year-old man has been coughing persistently for 3 weeks with a viral respiratory illness. He now develops sudden onset right lateral chest pain, severe on inspiration. His COPD is mild. X-ray shows a right 7th rib fracture. What is the specific mechanism of this fracture and how should it be managed?
options: Traumatic fracture from a fall — standard rib fracture management
Cough fracture (fatigue fracture from forceful repetitive coughing) — analgesia, treat the underlying cough cause, incentive spirometry; admission criteria should be assessed given age
Pathological fracture — urgent malignancy workup
Osteoporotic fragility fracture — anti-osteoporotic therapy only
explanation: Cough fractures: spontaneous rib fractures from repetitive forceful coughing — a fatigue/stress fracture mechanism. Common in: elderly patients, COPD, whooping cough, post-viral coughs, and those on long-term corticosteroids. Most common at ribs 5–9. Management: analgesia (NSAIDs + paracetamol ± opioids), treat the underlying cough, incentive spirometry, physiotherapy. Assess for osteoporosis — DXA and anti-osteoporotic therapy. Assess admission criteria: age alone in an 80-year-old with COPD and a rib fracture should trigger strong consideration of admission for monitoring and analgesia optimisation.

q: A patient presents with right-sided chest wall pain that has been present for 6 months. Multiple investigations including ECG, CXR, CT chest, and troponin are all normal. The pain is intermittent, sharp, and occurs in the right lower rib margin. Pressing a finger under the lower right rib margin and pulling anteriorly reproduces the exact pain. What is the diagnosis?
options: Costochondritis — NSAIDs and reassurance
Slipping rib syndrome — positive hooking manoeuvre; activity modification, physiotherapy, intercostal nerve block; surgical stabilisation for refractory cases
Fibromyalgia — multidisciplinary pain management
Atypical chest pain — refer to cardiology
explanation: Slipping rib syndrome (painful rib syndrome): hypermobility of the lower costal cartilages (8th–10th ribs) causing the anterior cartilaginous tips to slip under the rib above. Sharp, intermittent lower rib cage or upper abdominal pain — often misdiagnosed as biliary, GI, or cardiac pain. The hooking manoeuvre is diagnostic: examiner hooks fingers under the lower rib margin and pulls anteriorly — reproduces the pain and may reproduce the characteristic click/slip sensation. Management: reassurance, activity modification, physiotherapy, intercostal nerve block (diagnostic and therapeutic). Surgical stabilisation for refractory cases. Often misdiagnosed for years — making the diagnosis provides enormous reassurance.

q: Which analgesic approach is most evidence-based for severe rib fractures in a hospitalised patient?
options: Oral paracetamol alone — adequate for all rib fracture pain
Multimodal analgesia: regular paracetamol + NSAID + opioid as required; with intercostal nerve block or thoracic epidural for optimal analgesia and respiratory function
High-dose opioids only — most effective for severe pain
Chest binding combined with oral paracetamol — immobilisation reduces pain
explanation: Optimal rib fracture analgesia is multimodal: paracetamol 1g QID (regular) + NSAID (ibuprofen or ketorolac IV) + opioid PRN for breakthrough. Regional analgesia provides superior analgesia and improves respiratory outcomes: intercostal nerve blocks — effective for 1–3 consecutive ribs; thoracic epidural — gold standard for multiple rib fractures, provides bilateral analgesia, enables deep breathing and physiotherapy, reduces pneumonia and mortality in elderly patients. Chest binding is CONTRAINDICATED — increases atelectasis and pneumonia risk. Adequate analgesia is the single most important intervention in rib fracture management — it directly determines respiratory outcomes.

q: A 50-year-old presents with right-sided chest pain that started 2 days ago. A vesicular rash has appeared today along the right T5 dermatome. What is the treatment and what complication must be specifically discussed?
options: Topical aciclovir cream — sufficient for herpes zoster
Valaciclovir 1g orally three times daily for 7 days; discuss post-herpetic neuralgia risk and management; shingles vaccination for future prevention
IV aciclovir only — oral formulations are not effective
No treatment needed — herpes zoster is self-limiting
explanation: Herpes zoster treatment: antiviral within 72 hours of rash onset significantly reduces severity, duration, and post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) risk. Valaciclovir 1g TDS for 7 days (preferred — better bioavailability than aciclovir). PHN: persistent pain >3 months after rash resolution — occurs in 10–20% of patients, higher in elderly. Management: gabapentin, pregabalin, amitriptyline, duloxetine, topical lidocaine or capsaicin patch. Shingrix vaccine: highly effective (>90%) at preventing shingles recurrence and PHN — two doses recommended for adults ≥50. Ophthalmology referral urgently if ophthalmic distribution (herpes zoster ophthalmicus — risk of corneal ulceration and vision loss).

q: A 25-year-old male bodybuilder hears a pop while doing a heavy bench press. He develops immediate right anterior chest and axillary pain. He has weakness on resisted internal rotation of the right shoulder. Ecchymosis is developing over the right anterior chest and axilla. A defect is palpable at the anterior axillary fold. What is the diagnosis?
options: Anterior shoulder dislocation — shoulder reduction
Pectoralis major rupture — MRI or ultrasound to confirm; surgical repair recommended for complete rupture in active patients
Rib fracture — X-ray and analgesia
Costochondritis — NSAIDs and reassurance
explanation: Pectoralis major rupture: typically occurs during bench press — eccentric overload during heavy chest pressing. The tendon inserts on the humerus at the bicipital groove — rupture occurs most commonly at the musculotendinous junction or tendinous insertion. Classic presentation: sudden chest/axillary pain during bench press, weakness on resisted internal rotation and adduction, ecchymosis over the anterior chest and axilla, palpable defect at the anterior axillary fold. MRI or ultrasound confirms complete vs partial rupture. Complete rupture in active patients: surgical repair is recommended for best functional outcome — earlier surgery gives better results.

q: What is the hooking manoeuvre and what diagnosis does a positive result suggest?
options: Tapping over the carpal tunnel reproduces tingling — carpal tunnel syndrome
Hooking fingers under the lower rib margin and pulling anteriorly reproduces the patient's chest or abdominal pain — slipping rib syndrome
Sustained wrist flexion reproduces arm symptoms — Phalen's test for carpal tunnel syndrome
Passive dorsiflexion of the great toe reproduces heel pain — plantar fasciitis (Windlass test)
explanation: Hooking manoeuvre for slipping rib syndrome: examiner stands beside the patient, hooks their fingers under the lower rib margin (8th–10th ribs, anterior end), and pulls anteriorly and superiorly. A positive test reproduces the patient's typical pain — and often recreates the clicking or popping sensation the patient describes. This is the diagnostic test for slipping rib syndrome. The condition is often overlooked as a cause of chronic lower chest or upper abdominal pain because it is unfamiliar to many clinicians. Awareness of the diagnosis and application of the hooking manoeuvre is all that is needed — patients are often extremely relieved when their pain is finally reproduced and explained after months or years of investigation.

q: A patient with known malignancy (lung cancer) presents with new-onset right-sided chest wall pain that is constant, not reproduced by palpation, and present at rest and at night. CXR shows a subtle area of rib destruction. What diagnosis must be excluded and what is the appropriate investigation?
options: Costochondritis — NSAIDs and reassurance
Pathological rib fracture from bone metastasis — CT chest and ribs or bone scan; refer to oncology; pain management with appropriate analgesia including opioids if needed
Musculoskeletal strain — physiotherapy
Herpes zoster — check for rash
explanation: Constant chest wall pain NOT reproduced by palpation in a patient with known malignancy = pathological fracture from bone metastasis until proven otherwise. Red flags: constant pain, night pain, known malignancy, bony destruction on imaging. CT is the most sensitive for cortical bone destruction. Bone scan (whole body) assesses for other metastatic sites. Refer to oncology urgently. Pain management: regular analgesia following WHO analgesic ladder (paracetamol → NSAIDs → opioids), consider dexamethasone and zoledronic acid for bone pain. Palliative radiotherapy is highly effective for localised bone pain. Do not reassure MSK on examination findings alone in a cancer patient with new chest pain.

q: A 45-year-old male presents with acute onset left pleuritic chest pain and mild dyspnoea after a heavy lifting session. He is tall and thin. SpO2 is 95% on air. Breath sounds are reduced on the left. CXR shows a 20% left pneumothorax. He is haemodynamically stable. What is the management?
options: Immediate needle thoracocentesis — all pneumothorax requires emergency decompression
Small spontaneous pneumothorax in a haemodynamically stable patient — oxygen, observation, or aspiration; do not discharge without confirmation of resolution; refer to respiratory medicine or ED
Reassure and discharge — small pneumothorax always resolves spontaneously
Intercostal catheter (ICD) drain immediately
explanation: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP): occurs in tall, thin young males without underlying lung disease (bullae rupture). 20% pneumothorax with mild symptoms and haemodynamic stability: high-flow oxygen (accelerates nitrogen resorption), observation for 3–6 hours, aspiration if not resolving or significant symptoms. ICD for: large pneumothorax with symptoms, failed aspiration, secondary (underlying lung disease), bilateral, haemopneumothorax, or tension pneumothorax. Tension pneumothorax (tracheal deviation, haemodynamic instability, absent breath sounds) = immediate needle decompression, then ICD. Never discharge without confirmed resolution on repeat CXR. Recurrence risk 30% without pleurodesis.

q: A 60-year-old female presents with bilateral anterior chest wall pain and fatigue. She has 11 tender points on examination including bilateral anterior chest wall, bilateral trapezius, bilateral lateral epicondyles, bilateral greater trochanters, and bilateral medial knees. What is the diagnosis and management?
options: Bilateral costochondritis — bilateral corticosteroid injections

Fibromyalgia — multidisciplinary management: aerobic exercise program (strongest evidence), cognitive behavioural therapy, sleep management, low-dose amitriptyline or duloxetine; avoid prolonged opioid use
Rheumatoid arthritis — refer to rheumatology urgently
Multiple rib fractures — CT chest
explanation: Fibromyalgia: widespread musculoskeletal pain (≥3 months), multiple tender points, fatigue, sleep disturbance, cognitive difficulties, and associated anxiety/depression. Chest wall tenderness is common and may be the presenting complaint. Investigations: normal inflammatory markers (distinguishes from inflammatory arthritis), normal CXR. Management: patient education and validation, graded aerobic exercise (swimming, walking — most evidence), CBT, sleep hygiene, low-dose amitriptyline (10–25mg nocte — improves sleep and pain), duloxetine or pregabalin. Avoid prolonged opioids — worsen fibromyalgia outcomes.

q: Why is chest binding (strapping) contraindicated in rib fracture management?
options: It increases the risk of rib displacement
It restricts chest wall movement, reduces tidal volume, promotes atelectasis, and increases pneumonia risk — particularly dangerous in elderly patients and those with underlying lung disease
It causes skin pressure injuries
It is only contraindicated in athletes — safe for elderly patients
explanation: Chest binding is a historical practice that is now contraindicated in rib fracture management. Although it may temporarily reduce pain by restricting movement, it significantly worsens respiratory outcomes: reduced tidal volume → atelectasis → mucous plugging → pneumonia. This is particularly dangerous in elderly patients and those with COPD or other lung disease. Modern management prioritises adequate analgesia — enabling deep breathing and effective coughing — as the cornerstone of respiratory complication prevention. Incentive spirometry, chest physiotherapy, and early mobilisation complete the respiratory management.

q: A 40-year-old manual worker develops acute right lateral chest pain while lifting. He has severe point tenderness at the right 8th rib laterally. He is otherwise well, SpO2 99%, CXR shows a right 8th rib fracture with no pneumothorax or haemothorax, and pain is adequately controlled on NSAIDs and paracetamol. What is the appropriate disposition?
options: Mandatory hospital admission for all rib fractures

Discharge home with appropriate analgesia, written safety netting, and GP follow-up within 48–72 hours — young healthy patient with single rib fracture, adequate analgesia, no complications, and good SpO2
Intercostal catheter insertion before discharge
Refer to thoracic surgery urgently
explanation: Not all rib fractures require hospital admission. Outpatient management is appropriate for: young patient, single or 1–2 rib fractures, no underlying lung disease, pain adequately controlled with oral analgesia, SpO2 normal, no complications. Discharge with: NSAIDs + paracetamol ± short-term opioids for breakthrough, incentive spirometry instructions, activity modification, written safety netting. Return urgently if: increasing dyspnoea, SpO2 drops, pain uncontrolled, fever. Physiotherapy referral. GP follow-up within 48–72 hours. Contrast with elderly patients, COPD patients, or multiple fractures — these require admission regardless of initial SpO2 and pain control.

q: An 18-year-old female presents with left-sided sharp chest pain reproduced by pressing over the 4th left costochondral junction. ECG and CXR are normal. She has no systemic features and normal inflammatory markers. She is very anxious about her heart. What is the most important management step?
options: Troponin and 24-hour Holter monitor — must exclude all cardiac causes
Clear explanation that the diagnosis is costochondritis (a benign MSK condition), that the pain is not coming from her heart, and reassurance about prognosis — combined with NSAIDs and heat
Refer to cardiology — chest pain in a young female always requires specialist review
MRI chest — CT radiation not appropriate at this age
explanation: Reassurance is the most important therapeutic intervention in costochondritis — particularly for young patients who fear cardiac disease. Reproducible chest wall pain with a specific point tender on palpation, combined with normal ECG and no cardiac features, makes costochondritis the diagnosis. Providing a clear, confident, evidence-based explanation reduces anxiety significantly — often more than any medication. Explain: the costal cartilages are inflamed, this is not dangerous, and it will resolve. NSAIDs + heat for symptom management. Avoid over-investigating — additional tests driven by patient anxiety amplify health anxiety rather than reducing it.

q: A patient presents with chronic diffuse chest wall tenderness, moderate depression and anxiety on validated tools, widespread tenderness including the chest wall and bilateral trapezii, and very poor sleep. Inflammatory markers are normal. What is the most important aspect of management?
options: Extensive further investigation — fibromyalgia is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring many tests
Validate the diagnosis (fibromyalgia), address depression and anxiety, and prescribe an evidence-based treatment program: graded aerobic exercise + CBT + low-dose amitriptyline for sleep
Opioid analgesia — most effective for diffuse pain
Corticosteroid injection at each tender point
explanation: Fibromyalgia management: 1) Validation and explanation — acknowledging the reality of the pain and explaining the neurological mechanism (central sensitisation) is essential and often transformative. 2) Exercise — aerobic exercise (swimming, walking) has the strongest evidence; start low and build gradually. 3) CBT — addresses catastrophising, fear-avoidance, and pacing. 4) Sleep — amitriptyline 10–25mg nocte improves sleep quality and pain. 5) Duloxetine or venlafaxine for comorbid depression and fibromyalgia pain. Avoid: prolonged opioids (induce central sensitisation), benzodiazepines for sleep long-term, polypharmacy, excessive investigation.

q: A 30-year-old cyclist develops left lateral chest pain while cycling. He has point tenderness at the left 5th rib in the mid-axillary line. No dyspnoea, SpO2 99%, CXR is normal. He does not recall a fall. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Pulmonary embolism — CTPA
Intercostal muscle strain or stress reaction — RICE, NSAIDs, activity modification; if X-ray negative and pain persists, consider bone scan or CT for occult fracture
Spontaneous pneumothorax — observe
Herpes zoster — examine for rash
explanation: Intercostal muscle strain: relatively common in cycling (repetitive trunk rotation), rowing, and other trunk-intensive activities. Point tenderness over the intercostal space or rib with no trauma and normal CXR suggests muscle strain or stress reaction. Distinguishing features from rib fracture: strain tends to have tenderness over the intercostal space between ribs, no crepitus, and normal X-ray. However, stress fractures from repetitive loading can present with a normal initial X-ray. If pain does not improve with 1–2 weeks of rest and NSAIDs, arrange bone scan or CT to exclude occult fracture. Management: rest from cycling for 1–2 weeks, NSAIDs, gradual return with attention to bike fit.

q: A 55-year-old female on long-term prednisolone (15mg daily for 3 years) develops sudden onset right anterior chest pain when stretching to reach overhead. CXR appears normal. She has point tenderness at the right 4th rib anterolaterally. What additional investigation should be considered and what should be initiated?
options: Echocardiogram — prednisolone increases cardiac risk

Bone scan or CT rib — to detect occult fracture (X-ray misses rib fractures in 30–40% of cases); DXA scan for osteoporosis assessment; consider zoledronic acid or denosumab for corticosteroid-induced osteoporosis
MRI brain — prednisolone causes neurological complications
Reassure — chest pain on stretching is always musculoskeletal
explanation: Corticosteroid-induced osteoporosis significantly increases fragility fracture risk — including rib fractures from minor mechanisms (reaching, coughing, turning). Long-term prednisolone ≥5mg daily for ≥3 months requires osteoporosis prevention. CXR misses 30–40% of rib fractures — bone scan or CT rib should be considered if clinically suspected. DXA scan to quantify bone density loss. Corticosteroid-induced osteoporosis management: calcium + vitamin D supplementation, bisphosphonate (alendronate or zoledronic acid) or denosumab for significant bone density loss or high fracture risk. FRAX calculator (with adjustment for corticosteroid dose) guides treatment thresholds.

q: Which chest pain feature most strongly supports a musculoskeletal rather than cardiac diagnosis?
options: Chest pain occurring at rest — cardiac pain can occur at rest in unstable angina
Chest pain that is exactly reproduced by pressing on a specific point on the chest wall — this is the most specific musculoskeletal feature
Left-sided chest pain — cardiac pain is always left-sided
Chest pain lasting more than 30 minutes — distinguishes MI from angina
explanation: Exact reproduction of the presenting chest pain by palpation of a specific point on the chest wall is the most specific feature of musculoskeletal chest pain. When a patient says 'yes, that's exactly my pain' in response to targeted palpation — this is highly reassuring for MSK aetiology. Other MSK features: positional (worse with movement, rotation, deep breathing), non-exertional, associated with movement or activity, worsened by specific positions. These features support MSK diagnosis but always require cardiac exclusion first (ECG ± troponin) in appropriate patients.
